It peaks on a noun that names a component or subdivision of a structured object (body parts: chest, shoulder, neck, finger, muscle, tissue; subdivisions: line, page, row, string, set, piece, byte, scene), and on the ' of' of a partitive or measure construction where a portion/measure/collection noun is tied to the substance it portions out ('a bottle of water' 1.03, 'a kilogram of sugar' 1.27, 'two cups of flour' 0.76, '500 mg of amoxicillin' 1.58); a measure or unit noun also peaks when directly preceded by an expressed number ('5 meters' 1.56 vs 'meters' 0.16). It stays at its floor when the same head noun heads a genitive or property relation ('the colour of water' 0.02, 'the price of sugar' 0.00, 'the glass of the window' 0.04, 'the crust of bread' 0.11) and when a unit noun has no expressed number ('distances in meters' 0.18); a plain counted object after a number does not fire ('5 apples' 0.00).

adversarial_test_results.prompt: From the ridge the valley opened below us like a folded map, its fields stitched together by hedgerows and narrow lanes. We had walked since dawn, following a path the farmer had marked with red paint on the stiles. The air smelled of wet grass and woodsmoke, and somewhere below a dog barked at a passing tractor. My companion, who had grown up in the next village, named the farms as we passed them: Hollowcombe, Ashridge, and the long white house where the baker used to live. By midday the clouds had lifted and the whole vale glittered with rain. We stopped at a gate to share the last of the bread and the hard cheese we had bought in town, and to rest our legs on the smooth stone wall. The path dropped steeply after the gate, winding between hazel coppices that had been cut back the previous winter. Here and there a fallen trunk had been sawn and dragged to the side, and the fresh wood still smelled sharp and green. Patches of bluebells had gone over, their stems bending under the weight of seed, and the ground was soft with leaf mould. We crossed a stream on three flat stones that someone had laid long before either of us was born, and the water ran clear and cold over the pebbles. Beyond the stream the woods thinned into open pasture, where a herd of cattle stood in the shade of a single oak. A bull watched us from the far hedge without moving, and my companion said we should keep to the wall and not cut across the field. The path climbed again, steeper than before, and the sun came out properly for the first time that day. Sweat ran down my back, and I stopped twice to tighten a bootlace that had worked loose. Near the top of the rise we passed a ruined cottage, its roof gone and its doorway choked with nettles. Someone had scratched initials into the lintel, and a swallow had built in the corner where the chimney used to be. From there the path ran along the crest for a mile or more, with the sea visible in the distance and the smoke of a distant town hanging over the water. We ate lunch on a flat rock, and I boiled water on a small stove and made a flask of tea, which we drank while the wind pushed the grass flat around us. Later, at the bothy below the summit, a note in the logbook said the spring had run dry, so we carried three litres of water up from the stream and left a jar of honey and a sack of potatoes on the shelf for the next walkers. The light was going by the time we reached the road, and we walked the last stretch in silence, tired but content.
